## Probability Die is loaded given the number rolled

(1) You walk into the “occasionally dishonest casino” with prior probabilities and likelihoods set to the values in slides 21-25 of lecture #5. (that is, a “loaded” die has a 10% chance of getting a 1-5 and a 50% chance of getting a 6 but 99% of the dice are fair)

![](images/clipboard-1559043268.png)

```{r casino}
## priors
frequency_unloaded = .99 
frequency_loaded = .01

## for loaded die
p_6_given_loaded = .5 # P(six|D_loaded)
p_not_6_given_loaded = .5 # P(six_c|D_loaded) so .1*5=.5 there are 5 numbers other than 6 on a die

## for an unloaded dice
p_not_6_given_unloaded = 5/6 # P(six|D_unloaded)
p_6_given_unloaded = 1/6 # P(six_c|D_unloaded)


## probability 6 and loaded 
## P(6|L)*P(L) or P(L|6)*P(6)
p_6_and_loaded = p_6_given_loaded * frequency_loaded

## probability 6 and unloaded 
## P(6|UL)*P(UL) or P(UL|6)*P(6)
p_6_and_unloaded = p_6_given_unloaded * frequency_unloaded


## probability not 6 and loaded 
## P(N6|L)*P(L) or P(L|N6)*P(N6)
p_not_6_and_loaded = p_not_6_given_loaded * frequency_loaded

## probability not 6 and unloaded 
## P(N6|UL)*P(UL) or P(UL|N6)*P(N6)
p_not_6_and_unloaded = p_not_6_given_unloaded * frequency_unloaded

```

You pick up one die and with it roll:

2 3 2 6 3 5 6 2 6 6 2 6 6 2 3 6 6 6 5 6 6 5 6 6 6 6 6 4 6 3 3 3 6 6 5 6 6

Make a graph of the posterior probability that you have picked up a loaded die as a function of the number of times you have rolled the die.

-   If the roll value is NOT equal to 6, calculate P(L\|N6)

-   If the roll value is equal to 6 calculate P(L\|6)

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
rolls <-c(2,3,2,6,3,5,6,2,6,6,2,6,6,2,3,6,6,6,5,6,6,5,6,6,6,6,6,4,6,3,3,3,6,6,5,6,6)

# rolls <-c(2,3)

priors <- c(.01,.99) ## our belief aboout the frequency of unloaded die and frequency of loaded die
probloadedVec <- vector()

title = ""

for (i in 1:length(rolls)){
  probloadedVec[i] <- priors[1] ## we want to plot the probability that the die is loaded
  
  
  ## calculate the probability of the die being loaded given us not rolling a 6 (P(L|N6)) or not rolling a 6 (P(L|6)) 
  prob_loaded <- if (rolls[i] != 6){
    (p_not_6_given_loaded * priors[1])/( (p_not_6_given_loaded * priors[1]) + (p_not_6_given_unloaded * priors[2]) )
      }else{
      (p_6_given_loaded * priors[1]) / ( (p_6_given_loaded * priors[1]) + (p_6_given_unloaded * priors[2]) )} 
  
  
  ## calculate the probability of the die being unloaded given us not rolling a 6 (P(UL|N6)) or not rolling a 6 (P(UL|6))   
  prob_unloaded <- if (rolls[i] != 6){
    (p_not_6_given_unloaded * priors[2]) / ( (p_not_6_given_loaded * priors[1]) + (p_not_6_given_unloaded * priors[2]) )}else{
      (p_6_given_unloaded * priors[2]) / ( (p_6_given_loaded * priors[1]) + (p_6_given_unloaded * priors[2]) )} 
  

    
  priors[1] <- prob_loaded
  priors[2] <- prob_unloaded
  
  # print(priors[1])
  
  title <- paste(title, rolls[i], sep="")
  # plot(1:i, probloaded, main = title, ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(1,length(rolls)+1))
  # Sys.sleep(1)
}

plot(1:i, probloadedVec, main = title, ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(1,length(rolls)+1))

```

1.  How many times on average would you need to roll a loaded die to be 99.999% sure that it was loaded? (Show your work)

**You would have to roll the loaded die** **58 times to be sure it was loaded.**

**I make a function `rollLoadedDie` to simulate rolling a die 300 times. I then used bayes on the simulated data to determine how many times I would have to roll the die for the probability that it was loaded to reach 99.999%. After doing this 1,000 times, I can estimate that I would have to roll the die 58 times to know it was loaded.**

```{r}
rollLoadedDie <- function(numrolls){
  ## given a number of rolls, returns a simulated experiment
  
  final_vec <- sample(1:6, numrolls, prob = c(.1,.1,.1,.1,.1,.5), replace = TRUE)
  return(final_vec)
}

myRolls <- rollLoadedDie(30)
```

```{r}

bayesian_update <- function(rolls, priors, p_loaded, p_unloaded){
  probloadedVec <- vector()
  

  for (i in 1:length(rolls)){
  
    probloadedVec[i] <- priors[1] ## we want to plot the probability that the die is loaded

    ## calculate the probability of the die being loaded given us not rolling a 6 (P(L|N6)) or not rolling a 6 (P(L|6))
    prob_loaded <- if (rolls[i] != 6){
      (p_loaded[1] * priors[1])/( (p_loaded[1] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[1] * priors[2]) )
        }else{
        (p_loaded[2] * priors[1]) / ( (p_loaded[2] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[2] * priors[2]) )} 
    
    
    ## calculate the probability of the die being unloaded given us not rolling a 6 (P(UL|N6)) or not rolling a 6 (P(UL|6))   
    prob_unloaded <- if (rolls[i] != 6){
      (p_unloaded[1] * priors[2]) / ( (p_loaded[1] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[1] * priors[2]) )}else{
        (p_unloaded[2] * priors[2]) / ( (p_loaded[2] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[2] * priors[2]) )} 
    
  
      
    priors[1] <- prob_loaded
    priors[2] <- prob_unloaded
    
    title <- paste(title, rolls[i], sep="")
    # plot(1:i, probloaded, main = title, ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(1,length(rolls)+1))
    # Sys.sleep(1)
    if (probloadedVec[i] >=.99999){
      return(probloadedVec)
      break}
  }
  # plot(1:i, probloadedVec, main = title, ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(1,length(rolls)+1))

}
```

```{r}
# rolls <-c(2,3,2,6,3,5,6,2,6,6,2,6,6,2,3,6,6,6,5,6,6,5,6,6,6,6,6,4,6,3,3,3,6,6,5,6,6)


priors <- c(.01,.99) ## our belief aboout the frequency of unloaded die and frequency of loaded die
p_loaded <- c(0.5, 0.5) # p_not_6_given_loaded, p_6_given_loaded
p_unloaded <- c(5/6, 1/6) # p_not_6_given_unloaded, p_6_given_unloaded


bayes_experiments = vector(length = 1000)
for (i in 1:length(bayes_experiments)){
  rolls <- rollLoadedDie(300)
  bayes_experiments[i] <- length(bayesian_update(rolls, priors, p_loaded, p_unloaded))
}

sum(bayes_experiments)/length(bayes_experiments)
```

## Question 2

```{r}
simulateDisease <- function(numrolls, probs){
  ## given a number of rolls, returns a simulated experiment
  
  final_vec <- sample(1:2, numrolls, prob = c(probs), replace = TRUE)
  return(final_vec)
}

# myRolls <- rollLoadedDie(30)
```

```{r}

bayesian_update <- function(rolls, priors, p_loaded, p_unloaded, wanted_prob){
  probloadedVec <- vector()
  
  for (i in 1:length(rolls)){
  
    probloadedVec[i] <- if(wanted_prob == 1){priors[1]}else{priors[2]} ## we want to plot the probability that the die is loaded
    # probloadedVec[i] <- priors[1]
    
    ## calculate the probability of the die being loaded given us not rolling a 6 (P(L|N6)) or not rolling a 6 (P(L|6))
    prob_loaded <- if (rolls[i] == 1){
      (p_loaded[1] * priors[1])/( (p_loaded[1] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[1] * priors[2]) )
        }else{
        (p_loaded[2] * priors[1]) / ( (p_loaded[2] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[2] * priors[2]) )} 
    
    
    ## calculate the probability of the die being unloaded given us not rolling a 6 (P(UL|N6)) or not rolling a 6 (P(UL|6))   
    prob_unloaded <- if (rolls[i] == 1){
      (p_unloaded[1] * priors[2]) / ( (p_loaded[1] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[1] * priors[2]) )}else{
        (p_unloaded[2] * priors[2]) / ( (p_loaded[2] * priors[1]) + (p_unloaded[2] * priors[2]) )} 
    
  
      
    priors[1] <- prob_loaded
    priors[2] <- prob_unloaded
    
    # print(paste(rolls[i], ))
    
    # plot(1:i, probloaded, main = title, ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(1,length(rolls)+1))
    # Sys.sleep(1)
    if (probloadedVec[i] >=.99999){
      return(probloadedVec)
      break}
  }
  # plot(1:i, probloadedVec, main = title, ylim=c(0,1), xlim=c(1,length(rolls)+1))

}
```

Run simulations for a patient with the disease. About how many times on average must the test be repeated to achieve the hospital’s requirements?

**Around 15 times.**

```{r}

priors <- c(.001,.999) ## our belief aboout the frequency of no disease and frequency of disease ... loaded vs unloaded
p_disease <- c(0.09, 0.91) # p_negative_given_disease, p_positive_given_disease
p_nodisease <- c(.84, .16) # p_negative_given_no_disease, p_positive_given_no_disease

# p_loaded <- c(0.5, 0.5) # p_not_6_given_loaded, p_6_given_loaded
# p_unloaded <- c(5/6, 1/6) # p_not_6_given_unloaded, p_6_given_unloaded

bayes_experiments = vector(length = 10000)
for (i in 1:length(bayes_experiments)){
  outcome <- simulateDisease(100,p_disease)
  bayes_experiments[i] <- length(bayesian_update(outcome, priors, p_disease, p_nodisease, 1))
}

sum(bayes_experiments)/length(bayes_experiments)
# bayes_experiments
```

Repeat the simulations for a patient without the disease. About how many times on average must the test be repeated to achieve the hospital’s requirements?

**Around 4 times.**

```{r}

priors <- c(.001,.999) ## our belief aboout the frequency of no disease and frequency of disease ... loaded vs unloaded
p_disease <- c(0.09, 0.91) # p_negative_given_disease, p_positive_given_disease
p_nodisease <- c(.84, .16) # p_negative_given_no_disease, p_positive_given_no_disease

# p_loaded <- c(0.5, 0.5) # p_not_6_given_loaded, p_6_given_loaded
# p_unloaded <- c(5/6, 1/6) # p_not_6_given_unloaded, p_6_given_unloaded

bayes_experiments = vector(length = 1)
for (i in 1:length(bayes_experiments)){
  outcome <- simulateDisease(1000,p_nodisease)
  bayes_experiments[i] <- length(bayesian_update(outcome, priors, p_disease, p_nodisease, 2))
}

sum(bayes_experiments)/length(bayes_experiments)
```

(3) The hospital plans to run the test on one million patients per year. At a cost of \$1 per test, about how much should the hospital budget to run these tests? (That is to say, for a million patients, how many tests can the hospital anticipate running?)

    -   patient size: 1,000,000

    -   Of the 1,000,000 0.1% have the disease

        -   A positive patient must take the test \~15 times for 99.999% accuracy

    -   Of the 1,000,000 99.9% don't have the disease

        -   A negative patient must take the test \~4 times for 99.999% accuracy

    **It would cost 4,011,000 dollars**

```{r}

patients = 1000000
positive_patients = patients * .001
negative_patients = patients * .999

cost = (negative_patients * 4) + (positive_patients * 15)
cost
```
